summary: Weekly POC check-in focused on bridging SDK function-calling with orchestration patterns. Customers reported two recurring failures: malformed tool payloads and timeout cascades when downstream services are slow. Redwood SE outlined escape-hatch patterns (circuit breaker, local mock tool, structured fallback responses) and agreed to ship SDK examples. Action items: SDK snippets, staging benchmarks, and pricing/SOW for dedicated pilot.
questions: Will Redwood provide an SDK-level circuit-breaker or should we implement client-side?
How does prefix KV cache behave across canary rollouts?
What telemetry is available for per-tool cost attribution?
transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-12-19 15:00 UTC | Duration: 52 min | Recording: yes
Attendees: Jordan Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Desai (Redwood SE), Evan Li (Redwood CSM), Maya Soto (HelixMaps - Lead Platform Eng), Ben Harrington (CTO), Ravi Patel (ML Eng)

[00:00] Jordan Kim: Hey team, thanks for joining, this is Jordan, quick agenda — status on the invoke stability tests, review the SDK escape hatch patterns, and next steps for pilot sizing.
[00:12] Maya Soto: Hey Jordan, thanks. We ran the staging run last night, uh a couple things popped up. We saw malformed tool payloads about 0.8% of the time when we hit concurrency > 40.
[00:23] Ben Harrington: yeah and also we saw timeouts cascade to our orchestration layer, so requests that hit a slow backend would push the whole flow into errors.
[00:33] Priya Desai: Got it. Two separate failure classes — serialization/validation errors coming out of the function-calling layer and rippling timeouts. For the first one we usually recommend stricter output contracts plus an SDK-side validator and optional sanitization.
[00:46] Ravi Patel: quick Q, the payloads looked fine in raw logs most of the time, but sometimes the name keys were swapped - like tool_name vs toolId - does Redwood's function-calling normalize that?
[00:58] Priya Desai: The runtime tries best-effort normalization but yeah transcription of fields can vary. Our SDK includes a small shim that normalizes common flavors; we'll add a snippet for HelixMaps.
[01:12] Jordan Kim: And for the timeouts, the suggestion is circuit-breaker at the SDK layer, plus server-side per-route timeouts and a local mock tool so user flows get a graceful fallback.
[01:23] Maya Soto: We prefer SDK-level because we want client telemetry aggregated with request traces. Does Redwood surface per-tool trace IDs into the console?
[01:34] Evan Li: Yes — per-invoke trace IDs are supported and we'll link them to the route. You can see token breakdown and per-tool latency in the console — there's a short demo in the doc we shared, the link is in the notes.
[01:45] Ben Harrington: Also security — we need to confirm the VPC option and how KMS integration works for on-prem keys. SOC 2 is a must for procurement.
[01:57] Jordan Kim: Absolutely — we've got SOC 2 Type II, and the Private deployment supports customer-managed KMS/HSM. I'll attach the security packet.
[02:10] Maya Soto: thanks. Back to the SDK patterns — can you walk through the proposed escape hatch flow?
[02:18] Priya Desai: Sure. Step 1: SDK wraps function call with a short timeout and retry policy (exponential backoff with jitter). Step 2: if retries fail, SDK triggers a local fallback handler — either a canned response or calls a lightweight local microservice that returns best-effort output. Step 3: emit telemetry event and escalate to server-side circuit-breaker to drop traffic to that tool for X minutes. We'll show code.
[02:40] Ravi Patel: When you say server-side circuit-breaker, does that persist state across nodes, like a distributed breaker?
[02:48] Priya Desai: Yes, if you're on Dedicated or Private, the routing layer persists breaker state in our distributed metadata store; hosted has a lower TTL but still supports multi-node coordination.
[02:59] Ben Harrington: ok that helps. We also saw kv cache thrashing when canaries rolled out — small question: does the prefix KV cache invalidate on model or variant switch?
[03:11] Priya Desai: We invalidate per model-version by default; there's config to keep a warming cache for compatible variants. For canaries you can opt into a sticky prefix to avoid cold starts. But you trade memory for cross-variant contamination, depends on your acceptance criteria.
[03:28] Maya Soto: so we can keep warm cache for canary traffic only?
[03:30] Priya Desai: Exactly — route policy can pin canary traffic to warmed nodes.
[03:36] [02:36] (overlap/crosstalk) Jordan Kim: sorry timestamp drift there — moving on.
[03:40] Ravi Patel: On structured output — we ran a fail where model returned an array instead of the expected object and our parser threw. Any recommendations?
[03:51] Priya Desai: Strong typing + post-parse validator with recovery paths. Our SDK can auto-attempt coercion for trivial mismatches — e.g., wrap a bare array into an object if schema allows an items key — but we also recommend running eval prompt sets in staging to catch regressions.
[04:08] Maya Soto: could Redwood run a quick quality check on our prompt set? We can share the suite.
[04:14] Priya Desai: Yes, we can run a small eval against the pilot model and return the top failure buckets. We'll need the prompt set link and expected schema.
[04:22] Jordan Kim: Jordan to coordinate with Maya after the call.
[04:26] [05:00] Ben Harrington: pricing question — what's the incremental cost of enabling the dedicated pilot tier with persistent KV cache and higher SLOs?
[05:12] Jordan Kim: I'll send a draft SOW and pricing matrix. Short answer: resource premium plus small management fee; we can lock in a monthly commit that reduces unit costs.
[05:23] Maya Soto: procurement will want billing granularity and per-tool cost attribution. Is that available?
[05:29] Evan Li: Yes, we have token-level and per-invoke cost breakdown in the console and exportable CSVs for billing. We'll show an example.
[05:36] Ravi Patel: On telemetry, it would help to have sample traces with tool-level spans so we can map failures to our microservices.
[05:43] Priya Desai: The SDK emits spans compatible with OpenTelemetry and includes a tool span per function-call. We'll include an example config.
[05:54] [10:00] Maya Soto: Can we talk about the retry policy parameters? We saw retries sometimes made things worse during spikes.
[10:11] Priya Desai: Right — retries should be conservative. We recommend a single retry with linear backoff for low-latency requirements, or adaptive retries that inspect queue depth. For spikes, circuit-breaker thresholds must be lower than retry budgets.
[10:27] Ben Harrington: any guidance on batching vs latency for our use case? We do a lot of short-turn customer messages where latency is critical.
[10:36] Priya Desai: For short-turns, keep batch size small and prioritize low-latency routes; enable prefix/KV caching to reduce token generation. Batching is more for throughput-heavy async jobs.
[10:47] Maya Soto: do you have an example where batching improved cost without hurting latency significantly?
[10:52] Priya Desai: We have a bench doc — examples where micro-batch of 2-4 reduced per-token overhead on GPU by ~12% for seq lengths > 256 while keeping p95 latency withinSLO for certain hardware profiles. We'll link the bench.
[11:05] Jordan Kim: quick note: we'll add a small sample that toggles batch depth in the SDK so you can measure easily.
[11:12] [20:00] Ravi Patel: about the malformed payload — we traced it to a lib that mutates headers in one of our services, so fixing there should help, but we still want SDK guardrails.
[20:15] Priya Desai: Good, SDK guardrails plus a pre-send validator will reduce incidents. We'll include a preflight mode in the snippet to run validation without blocking for an initial window.
[20:27] Maya Soto: do you support dry-run mode in the hosted API? We want to exercise the call path without consuming tokens.
[20:36] Evan Li: We have a sandbox quota and a dry-run flag that returns simulated outputs for structural testing; it's not perfect for performance but good for schema validation.
[20:46] Ben Harrington: security again — will the dry-run data go to logs? We need assurance it doesn't leak PII.
[20:53] Jordan Kim: Dry-run is marked and excluded from analytics retention; but we'll confirm the exact retention policy in the security packet.
[21:02] [30:00] Priya Desai: For the SDK example I'll include three patterns: 1) validator + sanitizer; 2) circuit-breaker + retry; 3) fallback local mock. We'll show a small TypeScript and Python example.
[30:14] Maya Soto: great. Can you show how the SDK surface looks for registering a fallback? We have different microservices per region.
[30:22] Priya Desai: yes the SDK exposes registerFallback(toolName, handler) and you can supply region-aware handler selection. We'll share code.
[30:32] Ravi Patel: about observability — we want per-team dashboards in the console, is RBAC granular enough to hide some tool metrics?
[30:40] Evan Li: RBAC supports role and route-level scoping; you can hide tool or route metrics per team and integrate with your SSO via SAML.
[30:49] Ben Harrington: procurement will need the SLA language — p99 latency and uptime — can you provide sample SLA terms?
[30:58] Jordan Kim: yes, the Dedicated pilot includes SLO targets and credits for misses; I'll include a sample SLA clause in the SOW.
[31:06] Maya Soto: ok final — timeline. We want to run a 2-week dedicated pilot starting first week of January if we can get SOW and staging benchmarks by end of December.
[31:18] Jordan Kim: sounds reasonable. We'll aim to have SOW and code by 12/22 and Priya's SDK snippets by 12/21. Maya, you'll run the bench by 12/23.
[31:27] [40:00] (wrap-up) Jordan Kim: recap — Priya SDK examples; Jordan SOW and security packet; Maya bench results; Ravi verify parser. We'll reconvene next Friday same time. Any other blockers?
[40:40] Ben Harrington: none from procurement side right now.
[40:44] Maya Soto: just one more ask: can we get a short example of fail-open vs fail-closed behavior?
[40:50] Priya Desai: yes, we'll put both in the sample with tradeoffs. Fail-open returns best-effort content with a warning, fail-closed returns explicit error so downstream can handle.
[40:59] Jordan Kim: perfect — thanks everyone. Meeting adjourned.

Shared artifacts mentioned: https://redwood.app/poc/helixmaps/bridge-patterns (SDK snippets, eval bench, security packet)

End of transcript.
